rows.verified: Employers, people controlling dock premises, self-employed people and workers have health and safety duties under the Health and Safety at Work etc Act.
Anyone bringing dangerous goods into a harbour must pre-notify the harbour master or berth operator as required.
Harbour masters can regulate the movement of dangerous goods when they create health and safety risks.
Harbour authorities must maintain emergency plans for dangerous-goods incidents, and relevant containment incidents must be reported.
Dock traffic management should separate pedestrians and vehicles and provide hazard-free routes.
Port transport hazards include unsecured loads, reversing vehicles, limited visibility, open quay edges and mixed vehicle-pedestrian access.
Loading and unloading must be planned and carried out safely using maintained equipment, safe access, suitable lighting and rescue arrangements.
The Safety in Docks Approved Code of Practice supports dutyholders at both large ports and small harbours but does not replace compliance with other relevant health and safety law.
Port controls depend on cargo, vessels, shore-side roles, dangerous goods, traffic layout, lifting, quay edges, weather, access and emergency capability.
Ports evidence is operation-, cargo-, vessel- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level transport or major-incident probability.
The Quarries Regulations are intended to protect quarry workers and other people who may be affected by quarrying activities.
No one may work in a quarry unless competent or under the supervision of a competent person.
Quarry competence is based on relevant knowledge, experience, training and other qualities, not merely academic qualifications or length of service.
The quarry health and safety document should include risk assessments, management structure, emergency plans, rules, procedures and review arrangements.
Quarry design should minimise risks through appropriate faces, roadways, plant layout, tips, lagoons and public-protection measures.
Quarry operators are responsible for planning and preparation, day-to-day management, monitoring and review, with workforce participation.
Emergency plans should contain technical, operational and organisational measures to prevent dangerous situations escalating and to reduce harmful effects.
RIDDOR contains quarry-specific dangerous occurrences and requirements concerning notification, site disturbance and relevant equipment.
Quarry controls depend on geology, faces, tips, lagoons, explosives, mobile plant, roads, competence, public access, weather and inspection findings.
Quarry evidence is site-, operation- and geological-condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collapse or transport probability.
